title: Showcase: the flipped course
summary: The family secretly builds an obstacle-and-line course; the robot runs terrain it was never tuned for while they narrate its brain live, then they reveal the state diagram and name the person the free build is for.
materials: mBot v1.2 with the week 7 creature program loaded
their own practice line from week 7, for the pit lane check
black electrical tape and white poster board, handed to the family
a cereal box or similar for the family's obstacle, and cardboard for a dim tunnel
whiteboard and marker, face down until the reveal

steps.title: The tables turn
steps.body:
All season the family watched you build. Today it flips: they built, in secret, and your creature performs on terrain it has never seen. Somewhere in the house a course is waiting, taped and hidden, and you do not get to peek. If you saw any of it being built, say so honestly and look away from the rest.

The design loop still runs the day, just aimed at a new question. Ask: will the creature's rules hold on a course its builder never tuned for? Imagine: what could trip it? A curve tighter than your practice line, a light level its threshold never met, an obstacle at a strange angle. Plan: you cannot rehearse the course, so you rehearse the robot instead, in the pit lane step below.

One more thing turns today: you are the narrator now, not the driver. Once the robot starts, your hands stay off. Your job is to say out loud what its brain is doing, the moment it does it, and let the family judge whether the machine matches your story.

Hand the device to a grown-up when you reach the next step. It is addressed to them, not you, and a good showman does not read the other side's script.

steps.title: For the course builders only
steps.body:
Family, this step is yours. Build them a course they have never seen, and keep it hidden until showtime.

What to build, on the white poster board or a stretch of pale floor: a line course in black electrical tape, roughly two boards long, with at least two curves tighter than the practice line they made in week 7 and one good straight stretch. Somewhere on the line, stand one obstacle taller than the robot's front, a cereal box works, planted right in the path so the robot meets it face on. Somewhere else, make a dim stretch: a cardboard tunnel or bridge over the line, tall enough for the robot, dark enough inside to feel like evening.

What the robot can honestly sense, so your course plays fair: the two little eyes under its nose only tell it black or white directly beneath, so use the black tape on a pale background and make curves bends, not corners. Its distance sensor pings straight ahead in centimeters, so the obstacle must stand in the path, not beside it. Its light sensor feels the room's overall light, so the tunnel should genuinely dim things, not just decorate.

You may add one surprise of your own on top: a gap in the line, a dead end, a second obstacle. That surprise is the fun. Do not tell them any of it. During the show, watch the robot, listen to their narration, and afterwards each of you guesses one rule the creature was following before they reveal its brain.

Five minutes on your typing site while the family finishes their secret work, and no wandering off to peek. Warm up on the home row, then type the sprint's own words, ten times each, fast and without looking down: def, import, threshold, sensor, state. Every one of them lives inside the creature that performs today.

steps.title: Why a course you never tuned for is the honest test
steps.body:
Your thresholds came from data you collected in one room, on one day, under one lamp. The course waiting for you was built by other people, in its own light, with its own curves. That difference is the whole point of today.

A rule can pass a test two ways. It can remember: it works on the exact course it was tuned on, the way you can recite a poem without knowing what the words mean. Or it can generalize: it works on terrain nobody tuned it for, because the rule captured something true about the world, not just about that one afternoon. Running the robot on its own practice line only ever proves the first thing. Only a fresh course can prove the second, which is why scientists always keep back a test they never trained on.

So listen closely to what today's run really says. If the creature startles at the family's obstacle, the threshold your data chose was not a lucky number, it was a fact about how the sensor sees the world. And if a mood fires in the wrong place, that is not embarrassment, that is information: light differs from room to room and hour to hour, and a threshold measured under your lamp may sit wrong under theirs. Either way you learn something true, which is more than a rehearsed success ever teaches.

steps.title: Pit lane: rehearse the robot, not the course
steps.body:
A showman tests the machine the same day as the show. You cannot rehearse the course, so make the robot itself beyond suspicion.

Put in four fresh AA batteries; a tired battery makes motors slow and sensor readings strange, and today of all days the robot must be itself. Load the week 7 creature program and run it on your own practice line for two minutes.

Interview all three moods, one at a time. Roam: does it follow your line through the curve? Startled: slide your hand in front of the distance sensor and watch for the back-up and the yelp. Sleepy: cup your hands to dim the light sensor and listen for the snore, then press the button to wake it. If any mood misfires, this is the moment the bug diary earns its keep, not the middle of the show.

Last, set up the reveal: on the whiteboard, draw your three-mood state diagram from week 7, the moods, what sends the creature from each to each, and your two threshold numbers from your own data. Turn the whiteboard face down. It is the magician's secret, shown only after the family has guessed.
checklist: Fresh batteries are in and the week 7 program is loaded
All three moods fired correctly on the practice line, plus the button wake
Anything that misfired is in the bug diary with what fixed it
The state diagram and both thresholds are on the whiteboard, face down

figure.alt: The family's secret course: a line with a tight curve, a cereal-box obstacle planted directly in the path, a straight stretch, and a dim cardboard tunnel further along. A note explains why the course plays fair: the robot's eyes only see tape directly beneath them, its distance sensor pings straight ahead, and its light sensor feels the room's overall light.

items.s: Built in secret: tight curves, an obstacle in-path, a dim tunnel
Robot senses: tape under its eyes, distance straight ahead,

steps.title: The run and the reveal
steps.body:
Showtime. The family unveils the course. Take one slow look, out loud: say what you notice and what you predict before the robot moves. Tighter curves than yours? A tunnel? Name your worries in front of everyone; honest predictions are half the show.

Place the robot at the start and let go. From here your hands stay off and your voice does the work: narrate its brain live. Name the mood the moment it changes and say which sensor pulled the trigger. If it loses the line, gets stuck, or a mood fires where you did not expect, keep narrating exactly what its rules are doing, because a stuck robot obeying its rules is not broken, it is being honest. You may rescue it with your hands once, if the family agrees, and you must say what you are doing and why.

After the run, the guessing round: each family member says one rule they think the creature was following. Listen to all of them before you speak. Then flip the whiteboard and give the reveal: the three moods, what moves the creature between them, and the two threshold numbers your own data chose in week 6. Match each family guess to the diagram, right or wrong, and point at the exact spot on their course where each rule fired.

Close the reveal by answering the honest question: where did the creature generalize, and where did the family's terrain catch it? Say it plainly, wins and misses both. That sentence is the real trophy of the sprint.
checklist: I predicted out loud before the run and touched nothing during it, except at most one announced rescue
I named each mood change as it happened and the sensor that caused it
Every family member guessed a rule before the whiteboard turned over
The reveal matched each guess to the diagram and pointed at where each rule fired on their course
I said plainly where the creature generalized and where the new terrain caught it

steps.title: Name the person
steps.body:
The room is warm and the idea page is full. It opened in week 1 and every showcase has fed it since. Time for the season's promise: today you name the person your free build is for.

Fetch the page and read the whole list out loud, every person and every idea, even the silly ones. Silly week 2 scribbles have a way of growing up over a season.

Then choose the person, not the build. Say it to the room: the free build is for this person, and one sentence on why them. The build itself stays unchosen this week; in week 9 you will sketch three ideas for them, pick one, and pitch it with a real budget. A good season keeps its secrets on schedule, and this secret is now half open.

Write the person's name at the top of the page and circle it. From this moment the page belongs to them.
checklist: I read the whole idea page aloud to the family
I named one person and gave one sentence on why them
I did not pick the build idea; that is week 9's job
The person's name is written and circled at the top of the page

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A video of the run with your live narration, camera catching the course and the robot together. Keep rolling for the family's guesses and the whiteboard reveal if the camera can stay up, and end on the moment the person's name goes on the page.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
